title: Self-Test: Are You Offloading Your Thinking?
description: Seven honest questions about how you use AI. No right or wrong — but a mirror of who currently owns the process: you or the machine.

questions.text: You get a writing assignment on a topic that barely interests you. What happens?

options.text: The AI writes it, I hand it in. The topic isn't worth more.
I write a rough draft, then have the AI hunt for weaknesses.
I do everything myself. I don't touch AI for this.
The AI delivers an outline, I write the text myself.

questions.text: Exam in two weeks. How do you prepare?

options.text: I read AI summaries. Saves time.
I have the AI quiz me and generate mock exams.
Flashcards by hand, like always.
The AI explains what I don't understand — the testing I do myself.

questions.text: The recall check: can you say what's in the last text you submitted — without looking at it?

options.text: Honestly? No.
The arguments yes, the wording no.
Yes — I thought it and wrote it myself, after all.
Yes, even the passages where I disagreed with the AI.

questions.text: The AI gives you an answer that immediately makes sense to you. What do you do?

options.text: Take it. Sounds good, fits.
I ask back: "What speaks against this? What am I missing?"
I fundamentally distrust the answer and ignore it.
I spot-check one of its claims.

questions.text: A topic completely confuses you. Your first reaction?

options.text: Ask the AI for the finished explanation, tick it off, move on.
First sort out myself what I don't understand — then ask precisely.
Textbook, library, human. Confusion is part of learning.
I ask the AI to ask ME questions until it clicks.

questions.text: Your opinion on a contested issue — where does it really come from right now?

options.text: Honestly, often from what AI and feeds serve me.
I deliberately request the strongest counter-positions before I commit.
From conversations and my own experience — no tech involved.
I'm noticing right now: I don't actually know.

questions.text: If AI disappeared tomorrow — what would be your biggest loss?

options.text: I'd suddenly have to write everything myself again.
My training partner would be gone — contradiction at the push of a button.
No loss. More like a relief.
Research would get slower. My thinking would stay the same.

auslagern.title: Product Deliverer — someone else is doing the thinking right now
auslagern.description: Your results shine, but the process behind them belongs to you less and less. That's not a character flaw — it's the most convenient route, and AI is built to offer it to you. But: whoever hands over the process hands over the skill-building. The good news: this is reversible, with tools that contradict you instead of serving you.
auslagern.motto: You can hand over the product. Not the process.

sparring.title: Sparring Partner — you stay in the process
sparring.description: You use AI the way few people do: as a counterpart, not a ghostwriter. You have it quiz you, demand contradiction, keep the wording your own. That's exactly how ability grows instead of mere output. If you want to sharpen your sparring: the Atelier's tools are built for precisely that.

abstand.title: Keeping Your Distance — safe from offloading, but without a training partner
abstand.description: You don't hand over your thinking — which is more than most can say. But avoidance has a price: you're missing a training partner that contradicts you on demand, quizzes you, and hunts for your blind spots. Try Silent Mode: an AI that only ever asks questions. No risk, just friction.
